# Deuteronomy 34 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Authorship of the Chapter

Traditional Jewish and Christian commentators agree that Moses did not write this chapter. Gill notes that "Aben Ezra thinks Joshua wrote this verse by a spirit of prophecy; and it is very likely the whole chapter was written by him, and not the eight last verses only, as say the Jewish writers" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm). Guzik likewise states that unless Moses wrote it prophetically, "the most logical and uncomplicated explanation is that this chapter was written by someone such as Joshua or Eleazar the priest" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). Ligonier (Reformed) adds that "many scholars believe a later person, perhaps Ezra, added this note about Moses' prophetic office after Israel returned from exile" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/none-moses). PreceptAustin cites Geisler: it is "entirely reasonable to assume that someone, perhaps Joshua, added this final chapter" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary).

---

## v. 1: "Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which faces Jericho. And the LORD showed him the whole land—from Gilead as far as Dan..."

**The obedient ascent.** Guzik notes Moses was commanded in Deuteronomy 32:48–52 to climb Mount Nebo for his death; here that command was fulfilled. Moses began his work at one mountain (Sinai) and ended it at another (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). PreceptAustin observes: "Moses' ministry ends as it began—in the very presence of God! … As was typical of Moses, he obeyed God, this time even knowing he was going to his death" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary). Calvin, quoted at CCEL, wrote: "the ascent of Moses was equivalent to a voluntary going forth to death … such willing submission proceeded from no other source than faith in God's grace" (https://www.ccel.org/study/Deuteronomy_34:1-12).

**"Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah."** The Pulpit Commentary clarifies: "rather, unto Mount Nebo, the summit of Pisgah." Nebo was one peak in the Abarim range, with Pisgah as its highest point (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm). Gill agrees: "Nebo was one of the mountains of Abarim, which formed a ridge of them, and Pisgah was the highest point of Nebo" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**"The LORD showed him all the land."** The Pulpit Commentary insists this was not merely an ecstatic vision but that Moses' "power of vision [was] miraculously increased" because "this wide prospect could not be surveyed by any ordinary power of vision" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm). Gill concurs: "it can hardly be thought [his sight] should be so strong as to take a distinct view of the whole land of Canaan, to the utmost borders of it: no doubt but his natural sight was wonderfully strengthened and increased by the Lord" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm). Guzik sees this as "God's kind grace to Moses. Though he could not set foot in the Promised Land, God allowed him to see it" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**"Gilead as far as Dan."** The Pulpit Commentary notes this Dan is "not Dan Laish, near the central source of the Jordan … but another Dan in Northern Perea, the site of which has not yet been discovered (cf. Genesis 14:14)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm). PreceptAustin identifies Dan as "the farthest point north" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary).

---

## vv. 2–3: "all of Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the Western Sea, the Negev, and the region from the Valley of Jericho (the City of Palms) all the way to Zoar."

**The sweeping panorama.** Guzik notes the list follows "a large counterclockwise circle from the north to the south" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). Gill sees spiritual symbolism: Naphtali included "Galilee of the Gentiles, and so he had a sight of all that country most frequented by the Messiah when come" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**"The Western Sea"** — the Mediterranean. This is "the hinder sea" (Pulpit, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**"The City of Palms"** — Jericho. Gill notes it was "called, because of the multitude of palm trees which grew there," citing Josephus, Pliny, Diodorus Siculus, and Strabo as extra-biblical confirmations (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**Legal significance.** Guzik cites Thompson: "The invitation to Moses to view the land was not merely a kindly provision of God … There is some evidence that this was part of a legal process. A man 'viewed' what he was to possess" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). Guzik also cites Merrill: "The only time in Old Testament history that this ideal ever reached realization was in the heyday of the United Monarchy under David and Solomon" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

---

## v. 4: "And the LORD said to him, 'This is the land that I swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when I said, "I will give it to your descendants." I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it.'"

**God's faithfulness to the patriarchs, and discipline upon Moses.** God reaffirms His ancient oath to the patriarchs (Genesis 15:18; 26:3; 28:13). Gill notes the three references (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm). Guzik describes this as "a bittersweet moment" — Moses' heart thrilled at the sight, yet saddened because "it was his own sin – his own misrepresentation of God (Numbers 20:7-12) – which led to his not being able to set foot in the Promised Land himself. Here he stood so close, yet so far away" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Reformed reading:** Ligonier emphasizes that "death before entering Canaan was earthly discipline for Moses … Even the greatest old covenant prophet had to learn his place in the kingdom is through a grace that covers all his failures" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/none-moses). The same Ligonier devotional (R.C. Sproul's ministry) quotes the hymn "Rock of Ages": "Not the labors of my hands can fulfill the law's demands … all for sin could not atone; thou must save, and thou alone" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/none-moses). Ligonier's other devotional on the same passage speaks of Moses experiencing "seeing without proximity … believing without receiving … hoping without realizing" — yet insists it was not in vain, because "Moses actually made it to the real Promised Land: when he died, he met his God face to face" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/looking-promised-land).

**Christological contrast.** Guzik draws a pointed contrast: "Moses died under the penalty of sin, but his own sin … Jesus also died under the penalty of sin, but not His own … As great as Moses was, Jesus is the One greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:1-6)" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Spurgeon's reflection** (cited by Guzik): "His death leaves nothing to regret … Failing to pass over Jordan seems a mere pin's prick, in presence of the honours which surrounded his departing hours. His death was the climax of his life" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

---

## v. 5: "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, as the LORD had said."

**"The servant of the LORD."** Guzik calls this Moses' epitaph. He lists what it was *not*: "Moses, prince of Egypt," "Moses, miracle worker," "Moses, prophet" — only "Moses the servant of the LORD." He comments: "To be satisfied with simply being the servant of the LORD is worthy and important … It is the happiest of all stations in life, for when the Master is glorified, the servant is satisfied" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**"According to the word of the LORD" — literally "upon the mouth of the LORD."** This phrase has generated a famous Jewish legend. Gill and Guzik both report that some ancient Jewish traditions (including Jarchi / Rashi) interpreted this as Moses dying by a kiss from God's mouth. Guzik relates: "The medieval Jewish rabbi Maimonides wrote that of the 903 different ways to die, this was the best" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). PreceptAustin cites David Roper: "The Hebrew means literally, 'Moses died … with the mouth of the Lord,' a phrase ancient rabbis translated, 'With the kiss of the Lord'" — then draws the tender image: "Is it too much to envision God bending over us on our final night on earth, tucking us in and kissing us goodnight?" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary).

**The Pulpit Commentary** firmly states the phrase "simply means 'by or according to the command of'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm), though it acknowledges the rabbinic interpretation: "The rabbins interpret this, 'by a kiss of the Lord' … i.e. as Maimonides explains it, Moses 'died in a moment of holiest joy in the knowledge and love of God.'"

**Gill** adds that some "Jewish writers affirm that he died not, but was translated to heaven" — but dismisses this: "it is clear he did die" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm). He dates Moses' death (following Jewish tradition) to the seventh of Adar, the same day as his birth, and notes Josephus claimed it was the first of Adar.

---

## v. 6: "And He buried him in a valley in the land of Moab facing Beth-peor, and no one to this day knows the location of his grave."

**Who buried Moses?** The Hebrew says "He buried him" — understood as God Himself. Gill notes: "Jarchi and so other Jewish writers say, the Lord buried him; it may be by the ministry of angels … it is very probable he was buried by Michael, and who is no other than the archangel … our Lord Jesus Christ" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm). Guzik allows that "God may have done this through a human agent, such as Joshua or Eleazar the priest" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Why the hidden grave?** Multiple reasons are proposed:

- **To prevent idolatry.** Guzik: "So that Israel would not worship Moses or his tomb" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). Ligonier agrees: "probably to guard against the people later building an idolatrous shrine to Moses" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/none-moses). Gill cites Ben Gersom: "lest, because of his miracles, succeeding generations should make a god of him and worship him" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).
- **To prevent disobedience.** Guzik: "So that Israel would not take the body of Moses into Canaan, in disobedience to God's command that he would not enter the Promised Land" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).
- **The Pulpit Commentary** quotes Stanley: "the first instance on record of the providential obliteration … of the 'holy places' of Palestine; the providential safeguard against their elevation to a sanctity which might endanger the real holiness of the history and religion" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**Jude 9 and the dispute over Moses' body.** Guzik connects this verse to Jude 9: "Michael the archangel, in contending with the devil, when he disputed about the body of Moses." He offers two theories: Satan wanted to use the body for idolatry, or Satan claimed a right to it because Moses had murdered the Egyptian (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). PreceptAustin notes the same: "Mount Nebo is also the likely site of the conflict between Satan and the archangel Michael over the body of Moses (Jude 1:9)" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary). Guzik further speculates: "God had another purpose for Moses' body, which Satan wanted to defeat: Moses appears in bodily form with Elijah … at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-3), and perhaps Moses and Elijah are the two witnesses of Revelation 11" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Spurgeon** is cited: "Whoever had such a burial as that of Moses? Angels contended over it … That body was not lost, for in due time it appeared on the Mount of Transfiguration, talking with Jesus" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**The Pulpit Commentary** suggests that "like Enoch and Elijah, he was transferred to the invisible world without seeing corruption. Hence his appearance along with Elijah in bodily form on the Mount of the Transfiguration" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).

---

## v. 7: "Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not weak, and his vitality had not diminished."

**The 120 years in three forties.** Guzik and PreceptAustin both note the neat threefold division: 40 years as prince of Egypt, 40 as shepherd in Midian, 40 leading Israel. Guzik: "The first two-thirds were in preparation for the last one-third. Moses was willing to let God prepare him for 80 years" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**"His eyes were not weak, and his vitality had not diminished."** The Pulpit Commentary explains the rare Hebrew word translated "natural force" (לֵחַ): "it is doubtless the subst. connected with the adj. לַח moist, fresh … It is used here of the natural juices of the body" — i.e., his body's moisture or freshness was not dried up (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm). Gill similarly: "his 'moisture' was not 'fled,' as it may be rendered, his radical moisture; he did not look withered and wrinkled, but plump and sleek" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**He did not die of old age.** Guzik is emphatic: "Moses was not hindered by physical infirmity, but by the command of God … He did not die from old age. He died because Israel was going into the Promised Land, and Moses could not go with them." He cites Merrill: "He did not fail to enter Canaan because he died, but he died because he failed to enter Canaan" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Contrast with Isaac and Jacob.** The studylight.org Kingcomments notes: "The eye of Moses is not dimmed. He still sees as sharp as in his youth. That is in contrast to Isaac (Genesis 27:1) and Jacob (Genesis 48:10)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/deuteronomy-34.html).

**Spiritual application.** PreceptAustin quotes F.B. Meyer: "He had seen plenty of sorrow and toil; but such was the simple power of his faith, in casting his burden on the Lord, that they had not worn him out in premature decay … God was his home, his help, his stay. He was nothing: God was all. Therefore his youth was renewed" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary).

---

## v. 8: "The Israelites grieved for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the time of weeping and mourning for Moses came to an end."

**Thirty days of mourning — same as Aaron.** Gill notes the parallel with Numbers 20:29, where Israel also mourned Aaron thirty days (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**Mourning ended — time to move on.** Guzik: "As great as Moses was, the days of mourning for him ended. It was time to move on. God's program did not end with Moses, nor does it end with any man. The torch was passed, and God's work continued" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Targum tradition.** Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan's chronology: mourning ended on the eighth of Nisan, on the ninth they prepared to march, on the tenth they crossed the Jordan, and on the sixteenth the manna ceased (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

---

## v. 9: "Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses."

**The spirit of wisdom.** Guzik, citing Kalland, explains this as "the equipment that makes it possible for one to do what the Lord delegates him to do. The skilled workmen who made the priestly garments for Aaron and his sons were given wisdom to make those garments (Exodus 28:3). The spirit of wisdom for Joshua was the military and administrative ability necessary for the task the Lord had laid on him as well as the spiritual wisdom to rely on and be committed to the Lord" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**Laying on of hands.** This act (Numbers 27:18–23) signified the transfer of leadership and was an enacted prayer. Guzik: "Moses' prayer for Joshua was answered. Joshua was indeed full of the spirit of wisdom" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). Gill calls it "a symbol of the government being committed to him … and expressive of prayer for him" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**Typology of Christ.** Gill sees Joshua as a type of Christ: "on whom the spirit of wisdom and understanding is said to rest, Isaiah 11:2" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

---

## vv. 10–12: "Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face …"

**The unique prophet.** The Pulpit Commentary states: "Moses was the founder and mediator of the old covenant. As long as this covenant was to last, no prophet could arise in Israel like unto Moses. There is but One who is worthy of greater honor than Moses, namely, the Apostle and High Priest of our profession … Jesus Christ, the Founder and Mediator of the new and everlasting covenant" (Keil, cited at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**"Whom the LORD knew face to face."** Guzik clarifies this "does not literally mean 'physical face to physical face,' but it has the idea of free and unhindered communication. Moses had a remarkably intimate relationship with God" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). The Pulpit Commentary cites Onkelos' Targum: "For the Lord was revealed to him face to face," and adds that "the knowledge here referred to was … that special knowledge by which men, being known of God, are made to know him (cf. 1 Corinthians 8:3)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**Three marks of Moses' uniqueness (Guzik):** (1) personal intimacy with God ("face to face"), (2) the number and kind of miraculous signs, (3) the power and authority with which he led Israel. Guzik: "There were greater rulers over Israel than Moses, greater leaders, greater prophets, and greater priests. But before the coming of Jesus Christ the Messiah, there was never one man who held all offices so gloriously as Moses did" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

**"All the signs and wonders … in the land of Egypt."** Gill notes a Jewish calculation: the prophets collectively wrought 74 miracles; Moses alone wrought or was associated with 76 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**"The great terror which Moses showed in the sight of all Israel."** The Pulpit Commentary and Gill suggest this refers either to the terror struck into the Egyptians, or the terror Israel felt at the giving of the law at Sinai (Exodus 19:16) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).

**Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** "no other period of old covenant history had the numbers and varieties of miracles as the days of Moses … the flurry of miracles in Moses' lifetime was unsurpassed until the ministry of Christ" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/none-moses).

---

## Traditions and Differences

### Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)
R.C. Sproul's ministry (Ligonier) stresses that Moses' death before entering Canaan was **earthly discipline for genuine sin** — yet also that Moses, like all saints, stood only by grace. "Even the greatest old covenant prophet had to learn his place in the kingdom is through a grace that covers all his failures" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/none-moses). The devotional "Looking into the Promised Land" frames Moses' experience as "seeing without proximity … believing without receiving … hoping without realizing" — resolved by the truth that Moses "actually made it to the real Promised Land" at death (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/looking-promised-land).

### Baptist
Guzik (EnduringWord, broadly evangelical/Baptist) emphasizes that Moses died for his own sin and remained buried, contrasting him with Christ who died for others' sins and rose (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). The Baptist teacher Warren Wiersbe (cited at PreceptAustin) draws practical life lessons: "Moses lived in the heights, and he died in the heights … Moses lived in God's will and died in God's will. You never have to fear life or death if you walk in obedience to the Lord" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-34-commentary). Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) calls Moses' death "the climax of his life" and reflects tenderly on God kissing away Moses' soul (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (EnduringWord)
David Guzik's commentary is also widely used in charismatic circles. Guzik's treatment of Jude 9 and the transfiguration is particularly attentive to spiritual warfare: Satan contended for Moses' body, but Michael prevailed. Guzik raises the possibility that Moses and Elijah are the two witnesses of Revelation 11 — a view popular in some charismatic and premillennial circles (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

### Lutheran
No distinctively Lutheran commentary on this chapter was retrieved from the specified sources. The search at lcms.org and 1517.org did not yield results specific to Deuteronomy 34 within the search/fetch limits available.

## Other Views

### Jewish Tradition (cited by multiple Protestant sources)
- **Death by the kiss of God:** The phrase "according to the mouth of the LORD" (עַל־פִּי יְהוָה) was interpreted by rabbis as God drawing out Moses' soul with a kiss. Maimonides ranked this the gentlest of 903 ways to die. Guzik relays the full legend from Ginzberg's *Legends of the Jews*, in which God, with angels Michael, Gabriel, and Zagzagel, tenderly prepares Moses' deathbed and God Himself kisses his soul away (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/). The Pulpit Commentary acknowledges the tradition but demurs (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/34.htm).
- **Moses did not die:** Gill notes some Jewish writers "affirm that he died not, but was translated to heaven, where he ministers," but firmly rejects this: "it is clear he did die" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).

### Catholic and Orthodox
No results were retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org specifically on Deuteronomy 34 within the search limits available. 

### Modern Scholarship
No results from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org were retrieved within the search limits. Guzik, however, cites the modern scholar J.A. Thompson (a widely respected evangelical Old Testament scholar) regarding the legal significance of Moses' viewing of the land and the phrase "to go out and come in" as "a figure of speech" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-34/).

### The 1655 "Discovery" of Moses' Grave
Gill records that in October 1655, some Maronite shepherds claimed to have found Moses' grave on Mount Nebo with a Hebrew inscription reading "Moses the servant of the Lord," but "this story was confuted by Jecomas, a learned Jew, who proved it to be the grave of another Moses" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/34.htm).
